title: Supreme Court Revives Conviction & Life Sentence Of Ex-Congress MLA Vinay Kulkarni In 2016 Yogesh Goudar Murder Case
summary: The Supreme Court today set aside the Karnataka High Court order staying conviction and suspending life sentence of former Congress MLA Vinay Kulkarni for the murder of BJP Zilla Panchayat member.

note.Facts: Former Congress MLA Vinay Kulkarni was convicted by a Special Court for the 2016 murder of BJP Zilla Panchayat member Yogesh Goudar; the Karnataka High Court stayed the conviction and suspended his life sentence pending appeal.
note.Issue: Whether the High Court’s stay of conviction and suspension of life sentence for Kulkarni (and other convicts) is valid.
note.Held: The Supreme Court set aside the Karnataka High Court order, restoring Kulkarni’s conviction and life sentence, and also set aside the suspension of sentences of the other convicts.
note.Principle: A stay of conviction and suspension of sentence by a High Court is impermissible where the appellate court has not yet disposed of the criminal appeal, and the Supreme Court may restore the original conviction and sentence.
note.Provisions: Sections 143, 147, 148, 120-B, 302, 201 read with 149 of the IPC; Sections 25 read with 3, 5, 8 and 29 of the Arms Act, 1959; Special Court conviction; Karnataka High Court order; Supreme Court judgment.
note.Exam angle: Criminal Procedure Code – power of appellate courts to stay convictions and sentences; examine the conditions for granting a stay of conviction/sentence and the hierarchy of appeals (e.g., SLP, High Court, Supreme Court).

title: 'Cash For Jobs' Case: Supreme Court Directs Trial Court To Defer Proceedings Against Ex-TN Minister Senthil Balaji
case_name: Tamil Nadu Minister v. Senthil Balaji
summary: A bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana passed the direction after Senior Advocate Kapil Sibal, appearing for Balaji, informed the Court that the case was listed before the trial court for framing of charges. The State however denied that the matter was listed before the trial court for framing of charge.

note.Facts: Former Tamil Nadu Minister V Senthil Balaji is facing a corruption “cash-for-jobs” case; the trial court was scheduled to frame charges, but parties disputed the listing and sought adjournment.
note.Issue: Whether the Supreme Court should order the trial court to defer the proceedings pending further hearing.
note.Held: The Supreme Court directed the trial court to adjourn the matter to a date in the week commencing 14 December 2026.
note.Principle: The Court may defer trial-court proceedings when the issue before it is limited to bail and when premature charge-framing would prejudice the accused, emphasizing that serious allegations must not lead to condemnation without hearing.
note.Exam angle: Criminal Procedure Code (adjournment, framing of charges, bail) – could be asked on the scope of Supreme Court’s power to direct trial courts to defer proceedings or on the procedural safeguards against premature charge-framing.

title: Sale Deed For UP Property Registered Outside State After 1994 Amendment To Registration Act Is Void: Allahabad High Court
case_name: Dharmendra Kumar and another v. State Bank of India Central Office
summary: Allahabad High Court judgment in Dharmendra Kumar and another v. State Bank of India Central Office.

note.Facts: A sale deed concerning immovable property in Uttar Pradesh was registered by the Sub-Registrar at Mumbai after the 1994 amendment to the Registration Act.
note.Issue: Whether a registration of a Uttar Pradesh immovable-property document by a registrar outside the state is valid after the 1994 amendment.
note.Held: The registration is void because the Sub-Registrar at Mumbai lacks jurisdiction to register the document.
note.Principle: When the Registration (U.P. Amendment) Act, 1994 omits Section 30(2) and Section 67 of the Registration Act, 1908 for Uttar Pradesh, only a registrar within Uttar Pradesh can register documents relating to immovable property situated in that state; any registration outside the state is void.
note.Provisions: Registration (U.P. Amendment) Act, 1994; Section 30(2) and Section 67 of the Registration Act, 1908 (omitted for Uttar Pradesh).
note.Exam angle: Registration Act – jurisdiction of sub-registrars; could be asked to frame the issue of “jurisdiction of registration of immovable property” or to list the essential ingredients for valid registration under the amended Act.

title: Knanaya Christians Move Supreme Court Against Kerala HC Verdict Invalidating Excommunication For Marrying Outside Community
ratio: The balancing of denominational rights under Article 26(b) with other fundamental rights, particularly Article 21…
summary: A bench of Justice BV Nagarathna, Justice R Mahadevan and Justice Sanjeev Sachdeva listed the SLP on January 5 th , 2027 along with other SLPs against the HC judgment.

note.Facts: A suit filed in 2015 by Knanaya Catholics sought a declaration that a member would not lose Archeparchy membership for marrying outside the community; the trial court granted relief in 2021, which was upheld on appeal, but the Kerala High Court (HC) on 23 Mar 2026 held that endogamy is not an established custom or essential religious practice and ordered the Church to readmit excluded members, invoking fundamental rights against a non-State actor.
note.Issue: Whether the Knanaya community’s practice of endogamy qualifies as an essential religious practice/custom protected under Articles 26(b) and 29(1) of the Constitution, and whether the HC may subject such religious-denominational practices to Part III scrutiny and enforce mandatory injunctions against the Church.
note.Held: The Supreme Court has listed the Special Leave Petitions for hearing after the nine-judge Constitution Bench decides the Sabarimala reference; no substantive decision on the merits has been rendered yet.
note.Principle: The protection of a distinct religious denomination’s internal customs (including endogamy) under Article 26(b) and cultural rights under Article 29(1) must be balanced against fundamental rights, and the validity of the “essential religious practice” test and horizontal enforcement of fundamental rights against religious bodies remain to be determined by the Court.
note.Provisions: Constitution Arts 25, 26, 29 (including 26(b) & 29(1)); Indian Christian Marriage Act 1872; Cochin Christian Civil Marriage Act 1920; Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches Canons 6(2) & 1509; Specific Relief Act (referred); Sabarimala reference (Arts 25 & 26 interplay); Dawoodi Bohra excommunication reference (Art 26(b) vs Art 21).
note.Exam angle: Constitutional Law – test the scope of Articles 26 (b) (denominational autonomy) versus Articles 25/29 and Part III rights; possible question on “essential religious practice” test, horizontal enforcement of fundamental rights, or the applicability of specific relief provisions to religious injunctions.

title: Whether compelling disclosure of device passwords violate Article 20(3)? Supreme Court leaves issue to Delhi High Court
summary: Supreme Court: While considering a challenge to the Delhi High Court’s certain directions, including one on handing over electronic devices along with their passwords, a Division Bench of Ujjal Bhuyan and Atul S. Chandurkar, JJ., opined that since the matter is pending before the High Court, the High Court should decide whether compelling disclosure of.

note.Facts: The petitioner had an anticipatory bail application pending before the Delhi High Court and was under interim protection from arrest; the High Court directed him to hand over his laptop and mobile phone with passwords to the investigating officer.
note.Issue: Whether a court can compel an accused to disclose passwords of electronic devices, amounting to self-incrimination prohibited by Article 20(3) of the Constitution.
note.Held: The Supreme Court held that, since the matter is pending before the Delhi High Court, the High Court should decide the question of compelled password disclosure under Article 20(3). It also continued the petitioner’s interim protection from arrest until disposal of the anticipatory bail application.
note.Principle: When a legal issue concerning self-incrimination and compelled disclosure of passwords arises in a pending bail matter, the higher court may defer the decision to the lower court hearing the case, allowing it to determine whether such compulsion violates Article 20(3).
note.Provisions: Article 20(3) of the Constitution of India; Delhi High Court directions (paragraph 7); Supreme Court order disposing the SLP.
note.Exam angle: Article 20(3) – could be asked to frame the issue of whether compelled password disclosure is testimonial communication; examine the ingredients of self-incrimination and the role of higher courts in remanding such questions to lower courts.

title: Allahabad High Court Upholds 25-Year Sentence Of Man Convicted For Rape Of 5-Year-Old Girl
summary: Confirming the conviction under Section 376(2) IPC read with Section 6 of the POCSO Act , a bench of Justice Abdul Shahid said the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt through ocular and medical evidence.

note.Facts: The appellant was convicted for raping a 5-year-old girl in October 2013; the trial court sentenced him to 25 years’ rigorous imprisonment under Sec. 376(2) IPC read with Sec. 6 POCSO Act, based on the child’s testimony, corroborative family testimony and ocular-medical evidence.
note.Issue: Whether the conviction and 25-year sentence under Sec. 376(2) IPC read with Sec. 6 POCSO Act should be upheld.
note.Held: The Allahabad High Court affirmed the conviction and the 25-year term, dismissing the appeal.
note.Principle: When the prosecution proves rape of a child beyond reasonable doubt through consistent victim testimony, corroborative natural witnesses and medical evidence, the conviction and sentence under Sec. 376(2) IPC read with Sec. 6 POCSO Act stand.
note.Provisions: Sec. 376(2) Indian Penal Code; Sec. 6 Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act; no other statutes or cases cited.
note.Exam angle: POCSO Act – issues on admissibility of child testimony, corroboration, and sentencing under Sec. 6; could be asked to frame the ingredients of a conviction under Sec. 376(2) IPC/ Sec. 6 POCSO and the evidentiary standards required.
